nameStory: The 'lesser plait moss' gets its name from its small size compared to other plait mosses, and the distinctive pleated or folded appearance of its leaves when dry. The word 'plait' comes from the same root as 'pleat' - referring to how the leaves fold together like braided hair when moisture is scarce.
description: Lesser plait moss is a delicate, feathery moss that forms loose, irregular mats on tree bark and occasionally on rocks. The individual plants are quite small, typically only 1-2 inches long, with slender stems that branch irregularly. When moist, it has a soft, almost silky appearance with leaves that spread outward, but when dry it contracts into tight, twisted braids that look almost rope-like. It's one of the more inconspicuous mosses you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, irregular mats or grows in scattered patches on bark, never forming dense cushions like many other mosses

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves fold and twist into distinctive rope-like braids when dry - this pleated appearance is the key identifying feature and feels almost like tiny twisted silk threads

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Has a notably soft, silky feel when moist, quite different from the rougher texture of many bark-dwelling mosses

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-green when moist, becoming dull brownish-green when dry - overall much paler than most tree mosses

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring younger branches and twigs rather than rough trunk bark

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small, curved capsules on short stalks in late spring, but these are rarely seen due to the moss's inconspicuous nature

habitat: Lesser plait moss is found on the smooth bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's mixed and hardwood forests, from sea level to moderate elevations. It particularly favors younger trees and branches with smooth bark, such as young maples, birches, and beeches, avoiding the deeply furrowed bark of older trees. You'll most often spot it in mature forests with good humidity levels, especially in sheltered valleys and north-facing slopes.

seasonality.spring: Most visible in spring when frequent rains keep it hydrated and its pale green color stands out against dark tree bark. Sporophytes may be present in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Often contracted and dried during hot, dry periods, appearing as brownish twisted threads on bark that are easily overlooked.
seasonality.fall: Becomes more noticeable again with autumn rains, showing its characteristic pleated texture as it alternates between wet and dry conditions.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often hidden under snow or ice; on warmer winter days when moisture is available, it can show its silky green appearance.

funFact: Lesser plait moss can lose up to 95% of its water content and survive in a dormant state for months, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet - faster than a dry sponge soaking up water!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small feathery mosses on tree bark, but the distinctive rope-like braiding when dry is unique. Memory trick: 'Plaits like braids' - if the dried moss looks like tiny braided hair, you've found lesser plait moss.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: This species has very limited documentation in New England with only 8 recorded observations, so field identification should be verified by experts. Some details about this uncommon moss may need confirmation through additional research.**
compareHints: Since lesser plait moss is the only Jochenia species documented in New England, compare it with other small feathery bark mosses in the Hypnales order. Unlike the more common tree mosses such as Pylaisia or Entodon species, lesser plait moss has a distinctly paler color and more pronounced pleating when dry. Most other bark mosses don't show the same dramatic rope-like twisting that makes lesser plait moss distinctive.
